extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, classical political theory, and ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading and interpretation of Aristotle's Politics (chapters on the city, household, slavery, property, and money). The page lays out Aristotle's descriptive and normative criteria for what a city is, the nature of household relationships, types of acquisition, and judgments about money-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: City as natural and final cause
rubrics_metrics.description: A city is a natural production and contains in itself the end and perfection of government: first founded that we might live, but continued that we may live happily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle argues that when many villages join to form one society the result (a city) is the final cause and what is best; therefore the city is the work of nature and the proper telos of human association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Man is a political animal
rubrics_metrics.description: Man is naturally a political animal; speech (logos) proves that man is more social than bees or herding cattle and enables expression of what is just and unjust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because speech allows humans to communicate notions of good/evil and justice/injustice, participation in common sentiments via speech forms families and cities; this is a key criterion for why humans naturally form political communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of the whole (city) over parts (family/individual)
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of a city naturally precedes that of a family or an individual, for the whole must necessarily be prior to the parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle uses analogies (a man and his parts) to argue that an individual is understood by its 'energic qualities' and that a city is prior because an individual is not sufficient to compose a perfect government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family composition and its three distinct parts
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete family consists of freemen and slaves; the first and smallest parts of a family are the master and slave, the husband and wife, the father and child — the herile, the nuptial, and the paternal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle instructs examination of these three relations in order to understand household government and to separate provision (getting necessaries) from government of the family.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of mastership: knowledge versus law/force
rubrics_metrics.description: Some think the power of the master over his slave originates from superior knowledge (as with magistrate or king); others think domestic government is contrary to nature and established by law or force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle records competing accounts for the basis of mastership and prepares to evaluate whether the claim of natural mastership or the legal/forcible origin is justifiable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for natural slavery
rubrics_metrics.description: He who is by nature formed a slave is one who is qualified to become the chattel of another, who has reason enough to perceive that faculty but is not endowed with its use; such persons are slaves by nature and it is advantageous to them to be under government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle analogizes master/slave to soul/body and mind/appetite: where reason rules appetite it is natural and beneficial that some govern and others be governed; natural slavery is defended (with qualifications) on grounds of mutual utility and natural order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slavery by conquest (legal slavery) and justice
rubrics_metrics.description: A man may be a slave by law — a compact whereby those taken in battle are adjudged property of the conquerors — but many dispute the justice of this; victory often owes to superiority in advantageous circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle acknowledges the controversy: some justify slavery because law makes it so, others see it as unjust compulsion; he notes exceptions and debates about whether noble persons could justly be enslaved merely by conquest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between domestic government and political state
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestic government is a monarchy (what prevails in every house); a political state is the government of free men and equals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle emphasizes that governance appropriate to a household differs from that appropriate to a polity: the master's role is to employ slaves, not merely to possess them; the political state presupposes free, equal citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master's knowledge versus slave's knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: There is one sort of knowledge proper for a master (to employ his slaves properly) and another for a slave (practical household crafts and services).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The master should know how to order and apply servants; the slave's knowledge is of practical tasks. Masters who avoid low attentions hire stewards and attend to public affairs or philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property as instrument; slaves as animated instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Property is an instrument to living; an estate is a multitude of instruments; a slave is an animated instrument, whereas possessions can be used (not efficient causes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle distinguishes making from using: instruments are effici­ents of something else while possessions are used; slaves are instruments for use and may be considered parts in relation to the master.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural acquisition (economy) versus pecuniary/money-getting
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two species of acquisition: natural acquisition (procuring necessaries for the family — husbandry, hunting, war) which is part of economy; and pecuniary acquisition (trade, buying and selling) which is not the same and is not natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle argues natural acquisition has limits (providing what is necessary for a happy life), whereas pecuniary acquisition arises from exchange and can be limitless; the former is proper to economy, the latter to trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barter and the origin/use of money
rubrics_metrics.description: Barter arose when communities enlarged and had surplus/deficit; money was invented as a convenient medium of exchange (first valued by weight/size, later stamped).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Barter is not contrary to nature and is necessary for exchange among separated communities; money facilitates distant exchange and commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy's limits versus the limitless art of money-getting
rubrics_metrics.description: Economy (natural acquisition) has a boundary (the means necessary for a happy life), while money-getting (pecuniary acquisition) has no bounds because its object is money which can always be added to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle compares money-getting to medicine: the ends can be endlessly pursued even though means are limited; this difference explains why some prioritize wealth over living well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usury condemned as unnatural
rubrics_metrics.description: Usury (making money from money) is most reasonably detested, since it increases fortune by money itself and not by employing money for its natural purpose of exchange; TOKOS means 'breeding' of money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle treats usury as 'against nature' because money was intended as a medium of exchange, not as a growing, self-generating end; usury exemplifies the pathological end of money-getting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for excellent arts and occupations
rubrics_metrics.description: Arts are most excellent where chance has the least to do; the meanest arts deprave the body and are the most servile because they require chiefly bodily strength and little skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle values arts with skill and deliberation over those dominated by bodily labor or chance; this is used to evaluate the honorability and excellence of occupations (and indirectly where politicians and philosophers should focus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three parts of domestic government and roles of wife/children
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three parts of domestic government: masters, fathers, and husbands; the government of the wife and children should both be that of free persons but not the same — the wife as a citizen of a free state, the children under kingly power; the male is by nature superior to the female (except in unusual cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle prescribes different forms and expressions appropriate to each domestic relation and notes that in free states governors and governed may alternate; distinctions in honor and form should be observed between male and female roles.
